items.content_excerpt: A monthly overview of things you need to know as an architect or aspiring architect. Facilitating the Spread of Knowledge and Innovation in Professional Software Development Unlock the full InfoQ experience by logging in! Stay updated with your favorite authors and topics, engage with content, and download exclusive resources. Lily Mara explains how to avoid high-risk software rewrites through incremental FFI refactoring. She shares how engineering teams can replace Python bottlenecks with Rust via PyO3, demonstrating how to achieve dramatic function-level speedups, seamless integration testing, and meaningful infrastructure cost savings without microservice overhead. Agentic LLM systems have moved from linear prompt chains to graph-based workflows and, more recently, code-executing harnesses. Chains are simple but fragile, graphs add branching, retries, and validation, and code harnesses verify outputs through execution. The article advises validating model outputs and choosing the least complex design that meets reliability, speed, and cost needs. Manju Rajashekhar explains how the actor model solves the complex runtime challenges of production AI agents. By treating agents as distributed systems, he discusses state ownership, message passing, write-through state, and supervision boundaries to manage failures, continuations, and mutable execution graphs, moving agentic workflows beyond fragile demos to resilient architecture. Nathen Harvey shares insights from DORA research on AI adoption in software delivery. He explains why AI acts as an amplifier, how the DORA AI Capabilities Model drives outcomes, and why engineering leaders must evolve beyond bottlenecks like code reviews to achieve sustainable productivity, reduce delivery instability, and empower developers without burning out their teams. Andrew Martin discusses why AI security is fundamentally tied to Kubernetes security. He shares insights into the evolving AI threat landscape, covering non-deterministic agent behavior, GPU supply chain vulnerabilities, shared compute risks, and practical defense strategies - from prompt firewalling to agentic identity - to help secure cloud-native AI workloads in production environments. items.title: Post-Audit Mirage: Identifiability Limits of Offline Agent Verification
items.summary: Offline tests can fail to reveal whether an agent update will remain safe after deployment. We operationalize this post-audit mirage using matched safe and harmful lifecycles that expose identical verifier-visible evidence while an isolated scorer records opposite deployment truth. Our theorem applies standard observational-equivalence and indistinguishability ideas to this executable audit boundary and states the resulting error-abstention tradeoff. The Post-Audit Mirage benchmark makes that boundary executable across authorization, scheduling, and shared-capacity environments. IdentifiedRangeMonitor uses fresh group-labelled harm outcomes to return deploy, hold, cannot determine, or unsupported. Experiments show that monitoring can recover the missing distinction in favorable settings but may remain undecided for rare groups, small effects, or missing observations. Verifier-agent evaluation must therefore test both calculation validity and whether the available evidence supports the deployment decision.

items.title: Permission to Retry: A Study of Authorization and Recovery in AI Agent Workflows
items.summary: A durable agent can resume a consequential action while its authority changes and the action's external outcome remains uncertain. We study execution-time reliability of tool-using AI agents, isolating recovery decisions from language-model behavior. Checkpoint state, permission to dispatch, evidence of an external effect and permission to reconcile are distinct obligations. We present a finite conformance study that checks these obligations through histories scored against a provider effect ledger hidden from the recovering application. A prospectively frozen campaign executes 336 histories on native LangGraph and Temporal hosts, crossing 14 schedules, three provider contracts and four matched application policies. All 168 paired host cells have identical checked outcomes. Per host, retained-ledger reconciliation passes all 42 histories: 21 checked completions, 15 denials and six unknown outcomes with reservations retained. Cached retry, revalidation before retry and stable-key retry pass 30, 36 and 31 histories respectively. A separate 16-case component study of InfinityOS, an enterprise AI platform developed by Arya.ai, exercises exported authority, worker, recovery and settlement code over repository fakes. The results isolate the roles of current authority, provider contracts and retained observations in recovery, with safety, completion and unresolved obligations reported separately for the declared application profile.

items.title: Interpretable sparse fine-tuning with TopKLoRA enables faithful circuit discovery
items.summary: Fine-tuning on datasets of unknown origin can create a backdoor in the trained model when the data includes poisoned examples. Difficult to localise and remove, backdoors can persist through safety training. While parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods capture the full parameter changes introduced during training, they are not easily interpretable. We present the full method of TopKLoRA, extending the preliminary proposal of Masiak et al. (2025), an interpretable-by-design LoRA variant in which only the $k$ largest adapter latents are active at each token. Unlike SAEs, TopKLoRA is trained purely on downstream loss, where optimisation pressure incentivises learning functionally causal latents. We demonstrate this sparse LoRA adapter in a sleeper-agent backdoor case study where we create model organisms by fine-tuning gemma-2-2b, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Qwen2.5-7B on a poisoned instruction-following dataset. For each organism, we identify and ablate a circuit that is both necessary and sufficient to implement the backdoor. Furthermore, our new fine-tuning method produces sparse circuits that are up to an order of magnitude smaller than a dense LoRA baseline, allowing surgical ablation of the malicious capability without sacrificing instruction-following performance. Finally, we propose a technique to construct model organisms with localised circuits using TopKLoRA latents and gradient-routing, which we use to validate the findings of our circuit search algorithm. We consider these findings as a step toward interpretable-by-design architectures that provide faithful units of analysis without compromising model performance. We share our code: https://github.com/interpretable-finetuning/TopKLoRA.

Hand an agent a question and it’s left with a similar predicament: it has a limited context window, so like us humans, it has to retrieve information to complete certain tasks (instead of having everything memorized). It’s the job of an agent harness to apply these techniques strategically to get the model the right context at the right time for the given task. This blog covers the challenges with agent retrieval (finding and pulling in only the information necessary for the task at hand), the techniques at our disposal to combat them, and how to keep these in mind when designing an agent harness (using LangChain’s Deep Agents harness as an example). For more on how to manage context once it's in the context window, check out this blog on Context Engineering . items.title: Omni-UBench: Benchmarking Omni-Modal LLM-based Guardrails Across Safety, Utility, and Reliability
items.summary: Advances in Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs) have enabled increasingly seamless human-AI interaction, but their unified processing of heterogeneous modalities also expands the attack surface, allowing adversaries to exploit richer input compositions to circumvent safety alignment. To counter such risks, omni-modal guardrails have been proposed to detect and filter unsafe queries across arbitrary modalities. However, their capabilities and limitations remain insufficiently understood due to the absence of a comprehensive evaluation benchmark. In this paper, we present Omni-UBench, the first comprehensive framework for omni-modal safety assessment, evaluating guardrail models along three critical dimensions, i.e., safety, utility, and reliability. Omni-UBench curates over 183k samples drawn from 35+ heterogeneous sources spanning text, image, audio, video, and their cross-modal combinations, annotated with safety labels under a unified risk taxonomy. Benchmarking under Omni-UBench on 15 representative OLLMs and omni-modal guardrails yields several key findings, including: (1) modern OLLMs exhibit strong content moderation potential even without guardrail-specific tuning; (2) existing guardrails still struggle to identify cross-modal queries that conceal harmful intent or involve sophisticated jailbreaks; (3) they further exhibit substantial safety hallucination and over-sensitivity to textual patterns, revealing a deficient understanding of cross-modal safety semantics. Our findings provide valuable insights for developing more trustworthy omni-modal guardrails in future research.

items.title: Sustainability of TSFM Deployment and Pretraining: From Carbon Footprint Analysis to Mitigation via Pruning
items.summary: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) offer strong zero-shot forecasting capabilities, but their high pretraining cost raises a practical sustainability question: does this upfront investment pay off over a full deployment lifecycle, compared to supervised standalone models that must be periodically retrained? We model the cumulative carbon cost of different approaches across a realistic industrial scenario: Chronos-2 amortizes its pretraining cost within months for large or frequently queried deployments, but a classical model remains cheaper indefinitely for small or rarely queried ones. For cases where reducing the TSFM's own cost matters, we show that removing a single encoder block (7.9% of parameters) via a gradient-free pruning criterion yields a consistent 6 to 9% reduction in FLOPs, CO2 emissions, and latency, at essentially no cost to zero-shot forecasting performance across a 25-task benchmark.

items.title: How Legora runs 2,000 parallel agent evals on Modal Sandboxes
items.summary: To test a legal agent that works for hours across thousands of documents, Legora boots its entire application, pinned to a specific commit, inside a separate Modal Sandbox for every eval run.
items.story_key: model:modal|title:how legora runs 2 000 parallel agent evals on modal sandboxes
items.content_excerpt: Legora is an agentic system that supports lawyers in research, review, and drafting across complex matters. In early 2026, as rapid gains in model capabilities made longer and more autonomous legal work possible, Legora began replacing its existing AI assistant with a full-fledged agent. To test a legal agent that works for hours across thousands of documents, Legora boots its entire application, pinned to a specific commit, inside a separate Modal Sandbox for every eval run. The shift from assistant to agent exposed two major shortcomings in Legora's existing evals framework: scale and environment fidelity. The infrastructure challenge was to create thousands of isolated Legora environments in parallel, restore the right world into each one, and let the agent complete ambitious, long-running tasks. The first problem was scalability. The assistant had been designed for smaller tasks in environments containing a few documents. The new agent needed to run for hours inside a realistic project containing thousands of documents and gigabytes of data. Where the old eval system could run on a laptop, the new one needed to run in the cloud. The even harder problem was environment fidelity. Legora's agent spans their whole product: a headless DOCX editor, self-hosted Turbopuffer instances, PDF conversion, Postgres and authorization databases, blob storage, and dynamically created code-execution sandboxes. Today, each eval run executes in its own Modal Sandbox, loaded with a custom image and filesystem. While Legora evaluated multiple cloud-managed sandbox providers to replace local execution, they chose Modal for scalability, low startup latency, and support for complex environments. Each experiment kicks off 2,000 runs or more, each of which runs concurrently in a Modal Sandbox. Engineers on Legora’s team are able to kick off runs from their laptops to measure the impact of changes to their agent. To manage storage for each run, Legora uses Modal Volumes. Volumes make large document collections available across Sandboxes and let the team snapshot world state, deduplicating shared setup while ensuring that repeated runs begin from the same documents, database state, permissions, and blobs. The team also cached Docker images in Volumes to speed up the Docker Compose step, with plans to move that cache to filesystem snapshots. items.title: How Numan Built an Eval-First AI Health Coach with LangGraph and LangSmith
items.summary: How Numan built Nu, an AI health coach, on LangGraph and LangSmith with per-category evals, simulated conversations, and safety gates on a regulatory line.
items.story_key: model:langgraph|title:how numan built an eval first ai health coach with langgraph and langsmith
items.content_excerpt: Numan is a UK digital health company helping patients manage long-term conditions across weight, hormones, and sexual health. Many of our patients are on a weight-loss programme and use the app daily to track progress. When building Nu, our AI health coach, one of our design challenges was delivering high-quality health coaching without crossing the line into medical diagnosis, prescriptions, or making clinical decisions—all strict boundaries for agents in our highly regulated medical space. While we initially focused on the agent and automation around it, what turned out to matter most was the quality of our evaluation criteria. This is the story of how we developed and improved our evaluation criteria to deliver high-quality user experiences while steering clear of areas subject to regulation. We started where most teams start, with a dataset of inputs and expected outputs, and an LLM judge scoring each reply. While that playbook works well for a Q&A agent, coaching is a conversation, not an answer. Every approach that fixed Nu's reply in advance failed in two ways: 1. Single-turn evals on static fixtures (a fixed input, a fixed expected output, and a judge scoring one reply on its own). Behavioural coaching rarely has one right answer to a prompt and whether a reply was safe depends on the conversation around it. Nu needs to understand what is getting in the patient’s way across a conversation before it advises and hold the right boundary when a patient pushes. Averaging one score across the whole dataset hid where Nu failed. A few bad replies barely move the number, so the conversation looks compliant when it isn’t. The fixtures also caused a second problem. In one run, a cluster of low scores turned out to be the eval’s fault, not Nu’s. The rubric expected empathy, exploration and advice all within a two-turn exchange, whereas a human coach would pace these across a conversation. Nu was coaching properly, but the narrow, fixed eval signaled failures incorrectly. 2. Scripted multi-turn conversations. The obvious fix for single-turn fixtures is to write out a patient’s expected series of replies in advance. With this "script," several turns of a scenario, fed to Nu one at a time, allow the judge to score the full transcript at the end. While this gives the judge more room than a single reply, the eval fell apart the same way. Every organization has unique requirements for building and scaling generative AI. At Google Cloud, we are committed to giving developers model choice and architectural flexibility to run workloads however they need.

Today, we’re announcing the general availability of an Anthropic-managed deployment option for Claude Models on Google Cloud. This gives teams more choice in how they run their models, helping them consolidate AI workloads on Google Cloud alongside our existingGoogle-managed deployment option. 

Both options deliver the same frontier models on day zero, the same pricing, and the same Google Cloud billing. The difference comes down to who acts as your data processor and whether you need access to the new Claude platform features when they launch:

[NEW] Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed)

Delivers day-zero access to Claude models and Claude Platform features such as Claude Managed Agents (beta), skills, and code execution. Anthropic operates the stack as the data processor on Google Cloud infrastructure under Anthropic’s terms of service, while organizations authenticate with Google Cloud IAM, maintain Cloud Audit Logging, and consolidate spend under their existing Google Cloud billing and eligible commitments.

Learn more: Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic-managed).

Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed)

Continues to deliver day-zero access to the latest Claude models with strict governance, compliance, and sovereignty requirements. Google Cloud operates as the data processor under existing customer agreements, providing VPC Service Controls, Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK), and data residency in the U.S., EU, and APAC. New Claude Platform features roll out over time as they are integrated into the Google-managed infrastructure. items.summary:
v0.32.0

Highlights

This release features 814 commits from 363 contributors (121 new)!

  • Structured decisions and generic parsers: the new POST /v1/systemone endpoint answers choice, noul and score questions over a structured state (#59299), is served by default (#60677, #60696), and also runs on Cloudflare/clef-omni (#61064), LiquidAI/d1-3B (#60676) and DiffusionGemma (#60466). The new hf tool and reasoning parser (--tool-call-parser hf, --reasoning-parser hf) reads the checkpoint's response_template, so models that ship it need no model-specific parser (#58604, #58602), in both the Python and Rust frontends (#59005).
  • Low-precision KV cache everywhere: NVFP4 KV cache now runs on SM8x and SM12x (#46963), SM90 (#60620) and with XQA decode on SM12x (#60452), and on MiniMax-M3 sparse attention on SM100 (#59300); GLM-5.x defaults to an FP8 KV cache on SM100, halving KV memory per rank with 2.3-5.5% more throughput at a 7-11% TTFT cost in the PR's benchmark (#60140, #60281); fp8_ds_mla on SM90 gives GLM-5.3-Flash up to 31% more output throughput (#59246); ROCm gains the 4-bit ultraquant_4bit KV cache with about 2x the density of FP8 (#57057).
